title: Framework Laptop 13 Pro review: Much better battery, much worse price
gist: Framework's Laptop 13 Pro delivers the biggest battery-life and build-quality leap in the line's history via a redesigned chassis, Intel Panther Lake chips, and a shift to LPCAMM2 memory, but a supplier-driven doubling of LPCAMM2 prices amid an industry-wide RAM shortage pushes the machine to $1,500-$3,000, undercutting the value case for all but existing Framework owners doing partial upgrades.

insights.claim: The Framework Laptop 13 Pro is the closest thing to a second-generation redesign of the original Laptop 13, changing the bottom case, keyboard/trackpad input cover, and battery while retaining the motherboard, screen, and expansion-card system.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Signals Framework is willing to break backward compatibility selectively to fix long-standing design flaws while preserving its repairability pitch, a template for how modular-hardware vendors can refresh without abandoning their installed base.
insights.locator: Enter the Framework Laptop 13 Pro

insights.claim: A redesigned bottom case lets the Laptop 13 Pro fit a 74 WHr battery, up from 61 WHr in prior models and 55 WHr in the earliest generations, and in PCMark 10 Modern Office testing at 200 nits the laptop ran just over 18 hours, finally eliminating mediocre battery life as the line's biggest weakness.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: The single most-cited flaw of Framework's flagship laptop has been resolved, removing the main objection reviewers and buyers previously raised against the modular-laptop category.
insights.quote: far more than any previous Framework Laptop 13 and finally long enough to decisively eliminate “mediocre-to-poor battery life” as the laptop’s biggest downside.
insights.locator: Where Panther Lake really helps the Laptop 13 Pro shine is in battery life

insights.claim: The Laptop 13 Pro is Framework's first laptop fully machined out of extruded 6063 aluminum blocks and switches to a haptic (vibration-simulated) trackpad instead of a physical clicking mechanism, both aimed at matching the fit-and-finish of premium rivals like Apple's MacBook Air/Pro.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Build-quality parity with Apple removes another differentiator premium competitors used against Framework, strengthening its positioning in the higher end of the ultraportable market.
insights.locator: Framework says that the Laptop 13 Pro is its first to be “fully machined out of extruded blocks of 6063 aluminum,”

insights.claim: The Laptop 13 Pro's 13.5-inch, 2,880x1,920, 3:2 IPS display keeps prior specs but adds touch support (Framework's first), 700-nit typical brightness, an 1,800:1 contrast ratio, and an anti-glare coating, though it still lacks OLED and full DCI-P3 coverage and the review unit showed minor light bleed.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Incremental, not category-leading, display upgrade means Framework still trails premium rivals on panel technology even as it closes the gap elsewhere.
insights.locator: The final change of note is to the screen

insights.claim: No Framework Laptop 13 Pro configuration costs less than $1,500, and the reviewed configuration cost nearly $3,000, which the author calls expensive even by 2026's inflated consumer-tech pricing standards.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Pricing near premium ultraportable and even some workstation tiers narrows Framework's addressable market to enthusiasts and existing owners rather than mainstream buyers.
insights.quote: no model costs less than $1,500, and you’d spend nearly $3,000 to get the version I was sent for review.
insights.locator: The result is Framework’s nicest-looking, nicest-feeling, most polished laptop design

insights.claim: Framework's LPCAMM2 memory supplier recently doubled the price it charges Framework for the modules, and Framework is passing that increase on to most buyers who had not already placed Laptop 13 Pro preorders.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: A single-component supply shock (LPCAMM2 doubling) is directly inflating end-user pricing on a niche product line, illustrating how concentrated the LPCAMM2 supply chain still is and how exposed boutique PC makers are to component-cost volatility.
insights.quote: its supplier recently doubled the prices Framework was paying for LPCAMM2 modules, an increase Framework will be passing on to most people who haven’t already put in their Laptop 13 Pro preorders.
insights.locator: Framework isn’t the first laptop manufacturer to use LPCAMM2

insights.claim: A 32GB LPCAMM2 stick costs $800 directly from Framework, versus roughly $700 for one of the few available aftermarket sticks, a price the author calls steep even relative to the broader RAM shortage.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Concrete price benchmark for LPCAMM2 memory scarcity that investors tracking DRAM/memory-module supply chains can use to gauge how severe the current shortage is relative to standard DDR5.
insights.locator: A 32GB stick of LPCAMM2 costs $800 from Framework’s site

insights.claim: The author argues the Laptop 13 Pro's high price, driven by the RAM crisis, makes its real engineering improvements 'mostly theoretical' even for buyers who could have afforded Framework's older, lower prices, and calls the launch 'the right refresh at the wrong time.'
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: A best-in-class hardware refresh can still fail commercially if launched into a component-cost spike; timing risk from supply-chain conditions can outweigh product-quality gains.
insights.quote: it’s too bad that such a high price will make this laptop’s improvements mostly theoretical, even to people who could pay the prices Framework was charging a couple of years ago.
insights.locator: The right refresh at the wrong time

insights.claim: Framework switched the Core Ultra Series 3 motherboard from DDR5 SO-DIMMs to a single LPCAMM2 (LPDDR5X) module, which uses compression-attached copper contacts across one full side instead of a slot-and-edge design, and does not require matched module pairs for dual-channel speeds the way DDR4/DDR5 SO-DIMMs do.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Demonstrates a viable path to keep RAM user-upgradeable even as the industry moves toward soldered low-power memory for efficiency, relevant for any vendor weighing repairability versus power/performance tradeoffs.
insights.locator: If you haven’t heard of LPCAMM2 before, here are the basics

insights.claim: The move to LPCAMM2 was a technical necessity, not just a preference: Framework's higher-end Core Ultra Series 3 chips with fully enabled Intel Arc integrated GPUs do not support regular DDR5 at all, unlike the prior Intel and AMD generations Framework shipped, making LPCAMM2 the only upgradeable-memory option available.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Shows Intel's chip-level memory requirements are now dictating PC-maker design and cost structure, a supply-chain dependency investors in Intel's Panther Lake ecosystem should track.
insights.locator: But moving to LPCAMM2 was also something of a necessity for Framework

insights.claim: Framework skipped shipping a laptop with the prior Core Ultra Series 2 chip family entirely, likely because the most suitable Series 2 processors used memory integrated directly into the CPU package, which conflicts with Framework's stated preference against non-upgradeable RAM (already forced on it in the Framework Desktop).
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Illustrates how chip-package memory integration trends can force a repairability-focused vendor to skip entire product generations rather than compromise its core value proposition.
insights.locator: Framework didn’t ship a Core Ultra Series 2 laptop at all

insights.claim: Dell and Lenovo have already experimented with LPCAMM2 in a handful of laptops, but the format remains rare industry-wide, which is contributing to purchasing difficulty for both end users and Framework itself.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: LPCAMM2 adoption is still early-stage across the PC industry, meaning supply will likely stay tight and prices elevated until more OEMs commit volume to the format.
insights.locator: Framework isn’t the first laptop manufacturer to use LPCAMM2

insights.claim: On the Laptop 13 Pro, the 74 WHr battery, haptic-trackpad input cover, and new bottom case must all be upgraded together as a bundle; they are not individually compatible with older Laptop 13 batteries or bottom cases.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Existing owners face an all-or-nothing cost decision on the battery/chassis upgrade even though Framework markets modularity as a cost-saving feature.
insights.locator: If you’re looking for an easy rule of thumb

insights.claim: Motherboards, displays, and USB-C expansion cards remain interchangeable between the original Framework Laptop 13 and the Laptop 13 Pro, letting owners buy just a new Core Ultra Series 3 motherboard plus a CAMM memory module, or just the new touchscreen display, without replacing the whole chassis.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Partial upgrade paths meaningfully lower the cost of adoption for the installed base, a real differentiator versus sealed-design competitors and a mitigant to the otherwise steep sticker prices.
insights.locator: But motherboards, displays, and USB-C expansion cards are all interchangeable

insights.claim: Individual upgrade component prices: the 74 WHr battery is $89, the Input Cover Kit is $179, the Bottom Cover Kit is $169, the Touchscreen Display Kit is $299, the Panther Lake Core Ultra 5/Ultra X7 system board is $449/$899, and 16GB/32GB/64GB LPCAMM2 RAM is $239/$800/$1,600.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Gives investors and buyers a granular bill-of-materials-style price list for evaluating Framework's component economics and the disproportionate cost weight of memory in the upgrade bundle.
insights.locator: Here’s a non-comprehensive table listing the current prices

insights.claim: Every Framework Laptop 13 motherboard generation, including the original 11th-generation Intel Core board, already has updated BIOS firmware supporting the new Laptop 13 Pro hardware, a sharp improvement from years earlier when a battery capacity bump took months for some boards to receive compatible BIOS updates.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Faster, broader firmware support signals Framework's software/BIOS operations have matured, reducing a historical friction point that discouraged owners from adopting hardware upgrades.
insights.quote: any Framework board can become Pro.
insights.locator: It’s a mark of how far Framework has come in the last few years

insights.claim: Framework caps the Core Ultra X7 358H's sustained power at 30 W in Best Performance mode and 25 W in Balanced mode, well below the Asus Zenbook UX8407's 55 W sustained limit, so the Laptop 13 Pro underperforms that Asus in sustained CPU/GPU-heavy tasks like video encoding and gaming despite similar or better chip capability.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Framework is trading peak sustained performance for battery life and thermals via conservative power limits, a deliberate positioning choice investors should weigh against competitors that tune the same silicon more aggressively.
insights.locator: Nothing about the Laptop 13’s performance is too surprising

insights.claim: When the new Core Ultra Series 3 motherboard was paired with an older 61 WHr Framework battery, battery life still reached about 15 hours 45 minutes, showing that most of the Laptop 13 Pro's battery-life gain comes from the Panther Lake chip and LPCAMM2 memory rather than the larger battery alone.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Owners who only upgrade the motherboard (skipping the pricier battery/chassis bundle) still capture the bulk of the battery-life improvement, an efficient upgrade path for cost-conscious buyers.
insights.locator: Maybe unsurprisingly, the vast majority of the Laptop 13 Pro’s battery life

insights.claim: Testing the Ryzen AI 300 Framework board with the new 74 WHr battery yielded about 11 hours of runtime versus roughly 8.5 hours with the older 61 WHr battery, a gain roughly proportional to the capacity increase rather than a chip-driven leap like the Intel side showed.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Suggests the battery-life breakthrough is specific to the Intel Panther Lake platform's efficiency, not a universal effect of the new battery/chassis, which should temper expectations for AMD-board Framework buyers.
insights.locator: When testing the Ryzen AI 300 version of the Framework Laptop board

insights.claim: Framework is marketing the Laptop 13 Pro as a 'MacBook Pro for Linux users,' with Ubuntu 24.04 LTS available for the first time as a factory-preinstalled OS option, even though Framework has already officially supported Ubuntu and Fedora on prior Laptop 13 models.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Framework is explicitly courting Linux power users as a differentiated buyer segment Apple and most PC OEMs underserve, a niche-but-loyal market positioning distinct from mainstream Windows-first competitors.
insights.locator: The MacBook Pro for Linux users

insights.claim: Framework officially supports Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and Fedora 44 out of the box on the Laptop 13 Pro, lists CachyOS, Bazzite, Arch, and NixOS 26.05 as compatible community-supported distributions, and now delivers BIOS updates via LVFS instead of requiring a temporary Windows install as in earlier years.
insights.speaker: Andrew Cunningham
insights.so_what: Streamlined, distro-agnostic firmware delivery removes a longstanding practical barrier for Linux buyers, reinforcing Framework's Linux-friendly positioning with real operational follow-through rather than just marketing.
insights.locator: After a couple of bumpy years during which Linux users
